title: Vertices of the 120-cell with no three on a great circle
statement: The 120-cell is the regular four-dimensional polytope with 600 vertices on the unit sphere of R^4. Choose as many of its vertices as possible so that no three of them lie on a common great circle, that is, no three of the vertex vectors lie in a plane through the centre (in particular no two chosen vertices are opposite). The vertices come in 300 opposite pairs, which lie on 2,120 great circles through at least three pairs; 60 disjoint great decagons cover all of them, so at most 120 vertices can be chosen. Best known: 57 (ours).
submission: Text file: one line 'a b c d' per chosen vertex of the 120-cell, written as the tetrahedral cell of the 600-cell whose centre it is (four vertex numbers 0..119 of the 600-cell, numbered as in checkers/orig_codes.py).
score: the number of chosen vertices (larger is better)

best_known.source: Quantavane (Arhan Canli), 9 November 2026: random greedy choice followed by exchanges (a vertex whose only obstruction is one chosen vertex replaces it, then free vertices are added), many restarts (tools/greatcircle.py, mode search120)

context: The no-three-in-line problem asks for the most points of a grid with no three on a line (Dudeney 1917; Guy and Kelly 1968), and its projective form, caps, asks for the largest sets with no three collinear points in a projective space; over finite fields caps are a central topic of finite geometry. The 120-cell gives a real projective version with rich structure: its 600 vertices span 300 lines through the centre, and the great circles through three or more of its opposite pairs carry 6, 10 or 12 vertices (1,200, 720 and 200 such circles). A set with no three vertices on a great circle is a cap in this configuration. The Hopf fibration gives the upper bound: left multiplication by a unit quaternion of order 10 of the binary icosahedral group permutes the vertices in 60 orbits, each a great decagon, and a cap meets each decagon in at most two vertices, so at most 120. For the 600-cell (120 vertices, 12 decagons) the same bound is 24. How close a cap can come to the bound is open.
references: H. S. M. Coxeter, Regular Polytopes, 3rd ed., Dover (1973)
H. E. Dudeney, Amusements in Mathematics, Nelson (1917), problem 317
R. K. Guy, P. A. Kelly, The no-three-in-line problem, Canad. Math. Bull. 11 (1968) 527-531
J. W. P. Hirschfeld, Projective Geometries over Finite Fields, 2nd ed., Oxford University Press (1998)

novelty.verdict: new question: no-three-in-line problems are studied in grids and in finite projective spaces (caps); no result was found on vertices of the 120-cell or the 600-cell with no three on a great circle.
closest: The no-three-in-line problem in grids (Dudeney; Guy and Kelly) and caps in finite projective spaces (Hirschfeld): the same condition in other spaces.
Our other problems on the 600-cell (identifying codes, decycling, the Ising and Potts antiferromagnets): other questions on related polytopes.

baseline.text: 57 vertices, held by Quantavane (Arhan Canli), 9 November 2026: the set in `refs/cell120-great.txt`. Upper bound 120 (60 disjoint great decagons, at most two chosen vertices on each).

bound.source: the 60 orbits of left multiplication by an element of order 10 of the binary icosahedral group are disjoint great decagons covering all vertices, and each holds at most two chosen vertices
